1.point: The soul is the instrument of all our knowing and the one thing known directly, so the theory of irfan starts there; the Qur'an makes the whole human outcome turn on whether the soul is purified or betrayed.
steps: Irfan has a theoretical side and it begins with the soul
All knowing is done with the soul, so the instrument must be understood first
The soul is known by presence, and its knowledge of itself is the clearest case
The Qur'an (al-Shams) equips the soul with discernment and makes success and failure depend on what is done with it

2.point: The Qur'an links forgetting God to forgetting the soul and a ruined soul to lost faith; the hadith links knowing the soul to knowing its Lord; so God is known through the soul.
steps: Al-Hashr: forgetting God leads to forgetting the soul
Al-An'am from the other side: a ruined soul loses faith, because a soul that is seen points to its Maker
The saying 'whoever knows himself knows his Lord' states the positive direction
The soul reflects its Maker, so looking within is a way to know God

3.point: Meeting God is seeing one's own unveiled soul, a reflection of Him; it is nearness, not comprehension; God is already near, so the journey only lifts veils, and the road runs through the self.
steps: The Qur'an promises a meeting with God for every soul
The meeting is seeing the soul with its veils removed
The soul is a reflection, so the meeting shows a reflection, not God Himself
Neither the soul nor God can be known to the depths, so the meeting is nearness, never a grasp
Nearness is not distance: we are already in His presence, lacking only perception
The journey therefore removes veils rather than covering ground
Hence the way to God runs through the self

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: Sets up the theoretical side of irfan and states that it begins with the soul, the section's starting link.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Supplies the reason: all knowing is done with the soul, so the instrument must be understood first.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Supplies knowledge by presence and that the soul's contents, and the mystics' knowledge, are known this way.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Supplies the point's clause that the soul knows itself by presence, as the clearest case.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: Brings in al-Shams: the soul comes equipped with discernment, and sets up the verses on what follows.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Draws the conclusion from the verse: success and failure rest on the soul, so the human story is the soul's story; the Munajat line is a small side-link but the paragraph carries the step.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Links the last section to this one and frames al-Hashr as naming the cause of losing the soul.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: Reads the verse: forgetting the soul follows from forgetting God, and says what forgetting means; the punishment remark is a minor digression.

¶9.label: aside
¶9.why: The remedy by dhikr in stages is not used by any later paragraph; ¶12's 'both directions' rests on ¶8 and ¶11, not on this, and the point does not need it.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: Introduces the second verse, al-An'am, which supplies the soul-to-faith link from the other side.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: Explains why a ruined soul loses faith: a seen soul points to its Maker, the reasoning the point relies on.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Turns from forgetting to knowing and introduces the saying that ties knowing the soul to knowing its Lord.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Gives the saying's meaning, the soul reflects its Maker, which ¶17 later uses; the ruh remark is a small side-link.

¶14.label: restate
¶14.why: Tabataba'i's 'window of his own soul' says again what ¶13 already concluded, that God is known by looking within; a second authority with a new verse, no new step.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: Links knowing God through the soul to meeting Him and introduces the verse on liqa'.

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Defines liqa' Allah and supplies the step that the meeting is seeing the soul with its veils removed.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: Supplies that what is seen is a reflection of God, not God Himself, and why the verse still speaks of meeting Him.

¶18.label: advance
¶18.why: Supplies the limit: neither soul nor God can be known completely, the ground for 'never a grasp'.

¶19.label: aside
¶19.why: A puzzle about two readings of the saying, raised and set aside; ¶18 has already fixed the limit and nothing later uses the denial reading.

¶20.label: advance
¶20.why: Converts the limit into the term the rest of the section uses: the meeting is nearness, qurb, not a grasp; ¶21 picks it up. The Khomeini quotation is corroborative but the step is new.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Supplies that nearness is not distance: we are in His presence now and lack only perception.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: Supplies that the journey lifts veils and covers no distance; the cross-references to Chapter One, the prologue and Chapter Eight are dispensable but the step is needed.

¶23.label: restate
¶23.why: Summarises all three sections; every sentence repeats a conclusion already drawn (¶2, ¶4, ¶8, ¶11, ¶13, ¶16, ¶21-22).

¶24.label: aside
¶24.why: A question the chapter does not answer, a bridge to the next chapter; the section's argument uses nothing from it.
